_why:
Two edges, one of which is sourced largely by what its source does NOT contain.

l-san-agustin -> roswell-1947 is tier 3, and the Air Force's own 1995 records review is the right citation for it precisely because the Plains of San Agustin are not in it. 'The Roswell Report: Fact versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' is the USAF's answer to Congressman Schiff's request - an exhaustive search of Air Force archives, record centres and scientific facilities. Searched in full: 'San Agustin' appears zero times, 'Agustin' zero, 'Barnett' zero, 'Maltais' zero. The board's note already ended 'no primary document supports it'. The most authoritative primary review of the Roswell record contains no trace of the site, which is the strongest available support for that sentence.

What the same report DOES corroborate is the transmission chain in outline: 'In 1978... a UFO researcher, Stanton Friedman, met with Marcel and began investigating the claims', and 'two authors, William L. Moore and Charles Berlitz... publish a book, The Roswell Incident, in 1980. In this book they reported they interviewed a number of persons who claimed to have been present at Roswell in 1947 and professed to be either firsthand or secondhand witnesses'. Kevin Randle is named among the researchers. So the route by which the story travelled is documented; the site at the end of it is not.

A near miss worth recording: 'Newton' appears 21 times in that report and every occurrence is Maj. Irving Newton, USAF, the weather officer - not Silas Newton of the Aztec hoax. Matching on a surname would have produced a confident and completely wrong citation. Aztec and Scully appear zero times, so the report cannot source the Aztec edges either.

The Clarke edge corrects a title. The board had him as 'associate professor'. Sheffield Hallam's own research blog calls him 'Journalism Reader'.

sources.name: USAF, 'The Roswell Report: Fact versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' (1995), searched in full

edges.note: TIER 3, CONTESTED. The Plains of San Agustin entered the Roswell corpus through Grady 'Barney' Barnett's reported account, transmitted second-hand and published in Berlitz and Moore's 'The Roswell Incident' (1980). The Air Force's own 1995 records review corroborates the route the story travelled - it records that in 1978 'a UFO researcher, Stanton Friedman, met with Marcel and began investigating', and that Moore and Berlitz 'reported they interviewed a number of persons who claimed to have been present at Roswell in 1947 and professed to be either firsthand or secondhand witnesses'. It does not corroborate the site: 'San Agustin', 'Barnett' and 'Maltais' each appear zero times in the entire report. Kevin Randle, named in that review among the researchers, concludes on the evidence: 'It is for these reasons, that is the lack of first-hand corroboration of the Barnett tale, the inability of the first people to talk of what Barnett said to provide a location and date and that the only source of the information is Barnett that I say, with confidence, that nothing happened there in July 1947.' Roswell is July 1947, so that conclusion severs the link by dating rather than by geography.

sources.name: Sheffield Hallam University, C3RI Impact blog, 'Dr David Clarke presents UFO files at The National Archives', 8 March 2018
The National Archives, 'Unidentified Flying Objects (UFOs)' research guide

edges.note: Sheffield Hallam describes Clarke as its Journalism Reader and as 'media consultant and spokesperson for the transfer of 210 formerly classified files on UFOs from The Ministry of Defence archive' between 2008 and 2013. His own earlier role in prising the Rendlesham file loose is recorded at The National Archives by file reference: the guide notes that the Rendlesham papers were among the first released under the Code of Practice for Access to Government Information in 2001, and that the papers relating to that release sit at DEFE 24/2030/1 and DEFE 24/2031/1, catalogued as 'UFOs: Persistent Correspondence, Dr David Clarke, 2000-2001'. The custody relationship is documented in the archive's own catalogue entry, under his name.
